title: CRTC orders Bell, Rogers, Telus to stop charging prohibited wireless fees by Dec. 27
summary: Canada’s telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27.

image.caption: Canada’s telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada’s telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27.
Decision follows introduction of new hardware-related charges earlier this year
That includes fees for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) said in its decision on Friday.

In June, the CRTC banned internet and mobile providers from charging fees to activate, change, or cancel a service plan. Following that ban, major carriers introduced SIM- and other hardware-related charges that the CRTC flagged as potential disguised activation fees.

"We identified a number of fees charged by certain of the largest telephone companies that appeared to be prohibited. We notified them that the fees may be out of compliance," Sean Carter, the CRTC’s acting vice president of consumer analytics and strategy, told reporters at a virtual briefing on Friday.
"Since these companies chose to continue those fees, and they argued that they were not prohibited, we immediately took action to decide the issue."

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.
